title: Lease-based flow control and per-message timeouts for Go SDK streaming
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem
We currently depend on a single connection-level context timeout for long-lived streaming connections in the Go SDK. This leads to a few operational issues: (1) noisy cancellations when a single slow downstream consumer blocks the whole connection, (2) difficult-to-reason per-message deadlines for SDK consumers who need bounded latency for individual events, and (3) limited ability to throttle or shed load from the client side during bursts without tearing down streams.

Goals
- Introduce a lease-based flow control token to allow the server and SDK to communicate a consumer-specific message window that can be renewed independently of the primary stream context.
- Implement per-message timeout windows in the client so callers can set bounded latency expectations for single responses while keeping the connection open for subsequent messages.
- Ensure graceful shutdown semantics: SDK should be able to drain in-flight messages, emit partial results, and then close without triggering global cancellation for unrelated concurrent streams.
- Preserve ergonomics: keep the high-level streaming API familiar (ctx + stream.Read/Recv), but provide advanced hooks for flow-control and timeouts.

Proposal / Design summary
- Lease token: add an optional Lease struct that holds a TTL and available credits. The server may issue leases via a control frame. The SDK tracks the lease and only dispatches receive calls while credits exist. The SDK will expose an UpdateLease(ctx, lease) helper for users that want to drive flow control manually.
- Per-message deadline: the public streaming Recv API accepts an optional per-call timeout parameter (RecvWithTimeout(ctx, timeout)). Internally we create a per-message context derived from the parent connection context with its own deadline. This context will only control the specific message receipt, avoiding cancellation of the whole stream.
- Backpressure and jitter: implement a client-side smoothing window to avoid synchronized bursts when leases renew. Renewals will include jitter and a token refill policy (leaky-bucket analogue) shipped as default behavior.
- Shutdown & drain: add a CloseWithDrain(ctx, drainTimeout) method. When called, the SDK stops taking new consumer requests, enables an extended drain lease, waits up to drainTimeout for in-flight messages, flushes partial aggregations, and then closes the connection cleanly. If the drain period expires, remaining in-flight per-message contexts are cancelled but do not surface as global stream cancellation errors.

API sketches (Go)
- type Lease struct { TTL time.Duration; Credits int }
- func (s *Stream) RecvWithTimeout(ctx context.Context, msgTimeout time.Duration) (Message, error)
- func (s *Stream) UpdateLease(ctx context.Context, l Lease) error
- func (s *Stream) CloseWithDrain(ctx context.Context, drainTimeout time.Duration) error

Trade-offs considered
- Option A: Keep single connection deadline and add per-message timers in userland. Rejected because it forces every consumer to reimplement correct cancellation semantics and leads to more connection tears.
- Option B: Server-driven only leases with no client overrides. Rejected due to customer use-cases where clients need to prioritize messages locally (e.g., interactive UI vs background telemetry).
- Option C: Hybrid (chosen): Server may issue leases; SDK enforces them but exposes UpdateLease + RecvWithTimeout so advanced clients can balance global and per-message expectations.

Implementation plan (high level)
1) Wire low-level control frame parsing and new lease struct in runtime (backend interface unchanged). (ENG: infra/PR TBD)
2) Implement client tracking of lease state and leaky-bucket refill algorithm in stream manager component. Unit tests for refill and jitter.
3) Implement RecvWithTimeout and CloseWithDrain in Go SDK; add integration tests that simulate slow consumers and lease renewals.
4) Add examples and docs: Quickstart snippet showing RecvWithTimeout for UIs and UpdateLease for batch processors.
5) Rollout: feature-flag controlled for 2 weeks in sandbox, then enable by default after monitoring.

Testing and observability
- Unit tests for per-message cancellation to validate that cancelling a message context does not kill the connection.
- Integration harness that introduces artificial delays on individual messages and asserts that other messages continue to flow.
- Add SDK telemetry events: lease.acquire, lease.refill, recv.timeout, recv.cancel, drain.start, drain.end. These will be surfaced to Console retention-level metrics for debugging.

Migration and compatibility
- Backwards compatible: if server never sends leases and the client doesn't call UpdateLease, behavior is identical to today except RecvWithTimeout provides per-call timeouts.
- Clients with older SDKs will not understand lease control frames; servers must continue to support non-lease semantics until adoption is high.

Open questions / Risks
- Risk: differing perception of credit semantics between server and client. Mitigation: define an explicit state machine in design doc and test harness.
- Risk: developers misuse per-message timeouts and mis-handle partial aggregations. Mitigation: provide example patterns and lint rule suggestions in SDK docs.
